newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-LEYLAND SAYS HE WON'T RETURN TO PIRATES IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-LEYLAND SAYS HE WON'T RETURN TO PIRATES IN 1997.

text.p: Pittsburgh Pirates manager Jim Leyland, who led the team to three consecutive National League East titles from 1990 to 1992, said Tuesday that he will not return to the perenially cost-cutting team in 1997.
The Pirates said Leyland, 51, has been granted permission to speak to other teams.

"I think this is in the best interest for the Pittsburgh Pirates organisation and myself," said Leyland, who entered the season with a 776-771 managerial record. "It's time for a changing of the guard as far as the managerial position of the Pirates is concerned."
The Pirates are in last place in the National League Central Division with a record of 64-85, 15 1/2 games out of first place.
"Jim Leyland has asked for permission and we granted his request," said Pirates owner Kevin McClatchy. "The Pirates respect his wishes to speak with other clubs."
Leyland said he did not want to take anybody's job away or have any part of another rebuilding job. He would like to manage a team ready to make a title run.

"I will not pursue jobs where there is a manager in place. I will only talk to teams that do not have a manager under contract," he told KDKA TV in Pittsburgh. "I am not looking for a rebuilding situation. If that was the case, I'd stay in Pittsburgh. I love this city, this is where I made my home.

"I do not plan on managing for a long period of time. What I hope is to find an opportunity where I can be successful in the short run. I have two children and a wife that I hope to be able to spend a great deal of time with in the future and that time for me is not that far off."
Two possibilities are the Florida Marlins, where John Boles is serving as interim manager, and the California Angels, where John McNamara is doing the same.
Leyland, considered one of the game's most astute managers, may have become disenchanted with the rebuilding course the team was taking under McClatchy.
The new owner indicated to general manager Cam Bonifay that Bonifay would be allowed to increase the team's payroll in 1997, with the possibility of pursuing free agents.
This season, however, the Pirates have relied heavily on young players. They have used 21 pitchers, many of them rookies who Leyland has said are not ready to pitch in the major leagues.
The final straw may have come late last month, when the Pirates traded ace left-hander Denny Neagle to the pitching-rich Atlanta Braves for more young prospects.

"I want to make it perfectly clear that I was asked by Kevin McClatchy to stay on board," Leyland said. "It was a decision I had to make and it's a decision that, I feel, will be a positive step for the organisation and for myself."

"During the past few weeks, Cam Bonifay and I have had discussions with Jim Leyland," McClatchy said. "We made it clear to Jim that the organisation would like him to remain as the manager of the Pittsburgh Pirates."
Earlier this season, Leyland's contract was extended to the year 2000. Bonifay's pact was extended through 1998.

Leyland has managed the Pirates since 1986, the second longest continuous term behind Fred Clarke, who managed the club from 1900 to 1915. Leyland was bench coach for the Chicago White Sox under Tony La Russa from 1982 to 1985.
Leyland started with next to nothing when he was named manager of the Pirates, taking over a team that had lost 104 games the previous season and was mired in a drug scandal.
After finishing last in 1986, the Pirates under Leyland progressed to fourth in 1987 and second in 1988.

After a slip to fifth in 1989, Leyland's team strung together consecutive N.L. East titles from 1990 through 1992. In 1990, the Pirates lost to Cincinnati in six games in the League Championship Series.
The following two years, Pittsburgh played dramatic seven-game league championship series with the Atlanta Braves, losing both.

Even as they were winning, the Pirates were stripped of marquee players due to escalating salaries. Outfielder Bobby Bonilla left after the 1991 season and outfielder Barry Bonds and pitcher Doug Drabek left the following season, all via free agency.
By 1993, the Pirates had fallen into fifth place. In the strike-shortened 1994 season, Pittsburgh finished tied for third and were last in the National League Central last season.
